All these oro-dental features, summarized in Table 1 and Figure 1 and Figure 2, show common oro-dental manifestations in AML patients.

panels.rationale: Single peripheral blood smear panel showing a blast cell with an Auer rod, a classic morphologic finding of acute myeloid leukemia; caption and article context support AML attribution.
panels.attribution_text: Chadli et al. From Skin to Blood: Ulcerative Pyoderma Gangrenosum Unveiling Acute Myeloid Leukemia.. Cureus 2024. doi:10.7759/cureus.58838. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 3.
panels.figure_caption: Morphological aspect of a blast cell showing presence of Auer rod (arrow) on peripheral blood smear.
in_text_mentions: generative normocytic normochromic anemia (6.6 g/dL), leucopenia (2,400/mm3), neutropenia (1,250/mm3), lymphopenia (900/mm3), monocytopenia (150/mm3), basopenia (50/mm3), eosinopenia (50/mm3), and thrombopenia (25,000/mm3). Prothrombin time (PT:88%) and activated thromboplastin time (aPTT: 25sec) were within normal ranges. On the peripheral blood smear, 45% of blasts were observed, exhibiting irregular nuclei, microgranular cytoplasms, and occasional Auer rods (Figures 2, 3). Bone marrow aspiration was indicated; however, the patient persistently refused, even following psychiatric counseling.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Panel A is a Wright-Giemsa stained bone marrow smear from a patient whose marrow aspiration showed hypercellular marrow with 81% blasts and flow cytometry confirming AML (CD13+, CD33+, CD34+, CD117+). It visibly shows numerous large blasts consistent with myeloblasts, supporting the AML attribution. B: Panel B is the companion high-power bone marrow smear image (Wright-Giemsa, ×1000) showing a hypercellular marrow replaced by myeloblasts in a patient with confirmed acute myeloblastic leukemia; arrows highlight nucleoli and nucleated red cells.
panels.attribution_text: Wu et al. Acute myeloid leukemia presenting with gingival enlargement masked by a normal complete blood count: A case of delayed diagnosis and literature review.. Medicine 2025. doi:10.1097/md.0000000000046684. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 4.
panels.figure_caption: Images from the smears of bone marrow. The images show that the bone marrow is abnormal with acute myeloblastic leukemia. Bone marrow smear, Wright and Giemsa stain, ×1000 (A, B) (the blue arrow points to orthochromatic normoblast, the black arrows point to nucleoli, and the red arrows point to lymphoblasts).
in_text_mentions: a high index of suspicion for an underlying systemic malignancy. Consequently, despite the initially normal complete blood count, the patient was immediately referred for further hematological investigation. A repeated blood test was performed (at approximately day 30 post-initial visit), which revealed thrombocytopenia (68 × 109/L) (Table 1). Bone marrow aspiration demonstrated hypercellular marrow with 81% blasts (Fig. 4), and flow cytometry confirmed AML immunophenotype (CD13+, CD33+, CD34+, and CD117+). The patient received “7 + 3” induction chemotherapy with cytarabine and anthracycline.

in_text_mentions: proving serologic markers and worsening blood counts, she underwent a bone marrow biopsy to evaluate for an underlying marrow process. Bone marrow examination demonstrated AML with 61% blasts (Figure 2). Flow cytometry identified an abnormal blast population comprising 14% of analyzed cells that was CD45-dim with low side scatter and expressed CD34, CD117, CD13, CD33, and HLA-DR. Conventional cytogenetic analysis showed a normal female karyotype, 46,XX(20). Next-generation sequencing identified multiple mutations, including U2AF1, and the leukemia was classified as AML, myelodysplasia-related.

panels.attribution_text: Mitsumori et al. A New Histology-Based Prognostic Index for Acute Myeloid Leukemia: Preliminary Results for the "AML Urayasu Classification".. Journal of clinical medicine 2025. doi:10.3390/jcm14061989. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 4.
panels.figure_caption: (A). The results of immunohistochemical staining of the bone marrow at disease onset in a representative patient classified into Group 3 of the Urayasu classification for AML. Representative example of Group 1. The 38-year-old female patient with the t(8;21)(q22;q22.1) chromosomal abnormality. She was classified into the Favorable prognosis group by the ENL prognostic classification. The patient has maintained remission after induction therapy with cytarabine plus idarubicin. High-dose cytarabine was repeated thrice for consolidation. The patient has been in long-term first complete remission for 90 months. The results of immunohistochemical staining were as follows: P53(-)MRP1(-)AKR1B10(-)AKR1B1(-)CYP3A4(-)ENT1(+); remission induction therapy with cytarabine plus idarubicin, and high-dose cytarabine consolidation therapy were effective. (B). The results of immunohistochemical staining of the bone marrow at disease onset in a representative patient classified into Group 2 of the AML Urayasu classification. The red font indicates positivity, and the black font indicates negativity. HE is an abbreviation for hematoxylin–eosin stain. Representative example of Group 2. 70-year-old male patient with AML. Classified in the Intermediate prognosis group by ELN. There was a t(2;11) 11q23 chromosomal abnormality. First-line remission induction therapy with cytarabine plus idarubicin was ineffective, and second-line induction therapy with azacytidine plus venetoclax also proved ineffective. The immunohistochemical staining results were as follows: P53(+)MRP1(-)AKR1B10(+)AKR1B1(-)CYP3A4(-)ENT1(+). The treatment resistance was considered attributable to expressions of the tumor growth factor, P53, and of the idamycin-metabolizing enzyme, AKR1B10. (C). The results of immunohistochemical staining of the bone marrow at disease onset in a representative patient classified into Group 3 of the AML Urayasu classification. The red font indicates positivity, and the black font indicates negativity. HE is an abbreviation for hematoxylin–eosin stain. The patient was a 74-year-old female who was diagnosed as having a complex-karyotype AML and received combined idarubicin + cytarabine treatment as the initial remission-induction therapy, but CR was not achieved. As re-induction therapy, she received combined venetoclax + azacitidine treatment, but CR was not achieved, and the patient died three months later. Consent for autopsy could not be obtained. The patient showed tumor p53-positivity and was classified into Group 3. The tumor was MRP1-negative, AKR1B10-positive, and AKR1B1-negative. Her disease was resistant to the combined treatment with idarubicin + cytarabine as the initial remission-induction therapy. A possible reason for this is that her tumor cells were p53-positive and AKR1B10-positive/AKR1B1 (a competitive inhibitor of AKR1B10)-negative, which could have led to rapid metabolism of idarubicin within the AML blast cells, which was therefore no longer able to suppress tumor cell growth. The patient received combined venetoclax + azacitidine treatment as re-induction therapy for remission, but remission was not achieved. The reason for this may be that the venetoclax was rapidly metabolized within the AML blast cells due to an increase in the expression of CYP3A4, which metabolizes venetoclax.

source_variant.figure_caption: (A). The results of immunohistochemical staining of the bone marrow at disease onset in a representative patient classified into Group 3 of the Urayasu classification for AML. Representative example of Group 1. The 38-year-old female patient with the t(8;21)(q22;q22.1) chromosomal abnormality. She was classified into the Favorable prognosis group by the ENL prognostic classification. The patient has maintained remission after induction therapy with cytarabine plus idarubicin. High-dose cytarabine was repeated thrice for consolidation. The patient has been in long-term first complete remission for 90 months. The results of immunohistochemical staining were as follows: P53(-)MRP1(-)AKR1B10(-)AKR1B1(-)CYP3A4(-)ENT1(+); remission induction therapy with cytarabine plus idarubicin, and high-dose cytarabine consolidation therapy were effective. (B). The results of immunohistochemical staining of the bone marrow at disease onset in a representative patient classified into Group 2 of the AML Urayasu classification. The red font indicates positivity, and the black font indicates negativity. HE is an abbreviation for hematoxylin–eosin stain. Representative example of Group 2. 70-year-old male patient with AML. Classified in the Intermediate prognosis group by ELN. There was a t(2;11) 11q23 chromosomal abnormality. First-line remission induction therapy with cytarabine plus idarubicin was ineffective, and second-line induction therapy with azacytidine plus venetoclax also proved ineffective. The immunohistochemical staining results were as follows: P53(+)MRP1(-)AKR1B10(+)AKR1B1(-)CYP3A4(-)ENT1(+). The treatment resistance was considered attributable to expressions of the tumor growth factor, P53, and of the idamycin-metabolizing enzyme, AKR1B10. (C). The results of immunohistochemical staining of the bone marrow at disease onset in a representative patient classified into Group 3 of the AML Urayasu classification. The red font indicates positivity, and the black font indicates negativity. HE is an abbreviation for hematoxylin–eosin stain. The patient was a 74-year-old female who was diagnosed as having a complex-karyotype AML and received combined idarubicin + cytarabine treatment as the initial remission-induction therapy, but CR was not achieved. As re-induction therapy, she received combined venetoclax + azacitidine treatment, but CR was not achieved, and the patient died three months later. Consent for autopsy could not be obtained. The patient showed tumor p53-positivity and was classified into Group 3. The tumor was MRP1-negative, AKR1B10-positive, and AKR1B1-negative. Her disease was resistant to the combined treatment with idarubicin + cytarabine as the initial remission-induction therapy. A possible reason for this is that her tumor cells were p53-positive and AKR1B10-positive/AKR1B1 (a competitive inhibitor of AKR1B10)-negative, which could have led to rapid metabolism of idarubicin within the AML blast cells, which was therefore no longer able to suppress tumor cell growth. The patient received combined venetoclax + azacitidine treatment as re-induction therapy for remission, but remission was not achieved. The reason for this may be that the venetoclax was rapidly metabolized within the AML blast cells due to an increase in the expression of CYP3A4, which metabolizes venetoclax.

panels.figure_caption: Brain MRI (T1W, T2W, and FLAIR): A heterogeneous mass measuring 9 × 7.5 × 3 cm in the left temporal region, extending to the wing of the sphenoid and causing destruction of the lateral wall of the pilgrims, compressing the middle cerebral artery and infiltrating in the cavernous sinus.
in_text_mentions: The patient underwent several investigations, including a brain MRI revealed a massive heterogeneous mass 9 × 7.5 × 3 cm in the left sphenoid wing region. This mass exerted pressure on critical structures such as the carotid artery, optic nerve, and cavernous sinus (Figure 1).

8 , 9 While orbital involvement as an initial manifestation of AML is uncommon, it is less than 3% of cases. 10 In our case, brain MRI revealed a heterogeneous mass measuring 9 × 7.5 × 3 cm in the left temporal region, extending into the left sphenoid wing and causing destruction of the pilgrims. The mass compressed the left middle cerebral artery and bulged into the left cavernous sinus (Figure 1). MS can sometimes express B‐cell antigens (CD19 and CD79a), which may lead to misdiagnosis as CNS lymphoma. However, in our case, immunostaining confirmed AML with myeloperoxidase (MPO) positivity.

in_text_mentions: abilization and transfusion of two units of packed red blood cells, an emergency splenectomy was performed. Histopathological examination of the splenic specimen revealed globally preserved splenic architecture. The white pulp was composed of lymphoid aggregates surrounding arterioles, within which large blast-like cells were observed. The red pulp showed extensive hemorrhagic changes with marked vascular congestion. Immunohistochemical analysis demonstrated that the blast cells were positive for CD34 (Figure 2) and myeloperoxidase (MPO) (Figure 3), consistent with splenic infiltration by AML.

in_text_mentions: A biopsy extracted from the mesenteric lymph node was subjected to histopathological examination. The initial findings indicated the presence of an undifferentiated neoplasm. Subsequently, a diagnosis of myeloid sarcoma was established, parallel to the diagnosis of TMS. The confirmation of the diagnosis was achieved through the detection of MPO positivity on the lymph node (Figure 3). Diagnosing MS on a lymph node posed a challenge due to the absence of any prior history or suspicion of leukemia, which could have guided the pathologists toward suspecting it.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B, C, D). A: Panel A is a bone marrow aspirate (Wright–Giemsa, ×400) showing increased leukemic blasts in a patient with flow cytometry- and cytogenetics-confirmed AML, so it is a real patient histology image of the target disease. B: Panel B is an H&E bone marrow biopsy (×100) demonstrating increased leukemic blasts, a specific manifestation of the AML diagnosed in this patient. C: Panel C is CD34 immunohistochemistry (×200) of the bone marrow showing the leukemic blast population of this AML case. D: Panel D is myeloperoxidase immunohistochemistry (×200) confirming myeloid lineage of the leukemic blasts in this AML patient.

A bone marrow (BM) study revealed 20.8% blasts with decreased and dysplastic trilineage hematopoietic cells (Figure 2A–D). Flow cytometry revealed blasts expressing CD34 and positive for CD13, CD33, and CD117; weakly positive for MPO; and negative for other lineage–specific markers, including surface and cytoplasmic CD3, CD19, CD10, and cytoplasmic CD79a, a finding consistent with AML. panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B, C, D). A: H&E section of testis showing sheets of blasts in a patient with acute myeloid leukemia presenting as testicular myeloid sarcoma. [raw subtype: myeloid_sarcoma] B: High-power H&E of testicular myeloid sarcoma with arrows indicating blasts, supporting acute myeloid leukemia extramedullary involvement. [raw subtype: myeloid_sarcoma] C: CD117 immunohistochemistry highlights testicular myeloid sarcoma cells, supporting acute myeloid leukemia. [raw subtype: myeloid_sarcoma] D: Strong myeloperoxidase immunopositivity in tumor cells confirms myeloid lineage in testicular myeloid sarcoma associated with acute myeloid leukemia. [raw subtype: myeloid_sarcoma]

panels.figure_caption: Histopathological examination of the testis Panel A: Testicular parenchyma showing sheets of blasts. Panel B: Sheets of blasts, medium-sized cells with an increased nuclear-cytoplasmic ratio, in a high-power field (H&E, x100). Panel C: CD117 immunopositivity in tumor cells (x100). Panel D: Strong MPO positivity (x100).
in_text_mentions: stology and immunohistochemistry. On cross-section, the gray-white firm mass measured 7.5x5x3.2 cm (Figure 1). The histology report of the mass shows testicular parenchyma with seminiferous tubules interspersed and surrounded by intermediate- to large-sized neoplastic cells with scant cytoplasm arranged in sheets. Immunohistochemistry demonstrated a strong positive for CD45, CD34, CD117, and myeloperoxidase (MPO) (Figure 2). In contrast, it was negative for ALK-1, Tdt, CD99, CD3, CD1a, CD10, CD19, CD20, Inhibin, and desmin. These results suggest a diagnosis of testicular myeloid sarcoma (TMS).

panels.rationale: Single H&E histology panel from a patient with relapsed acute myeloid leukemia, showing diffuse infiltration of the left mastoid bone by medium- and large-sized cells with irregular nuclei and scant cytoplasm, with immunohistochemistry confirming myeloblasts (MPO, CD34, TdT, CD117, CD68 positive). This supports AML involving an extramedullary/mastoid site.

in_text_mentions: found to account for 92.8%, which had relatively regular bodies and nucleus, and some natiform or butterfly-shaped nucleus were occasionally observed. The cells had less cytoplasm, few or no granules, less inner and outer cytoplasm in individual cells, and occasional Auer bodies. findings.label: Hepatosplenomegaly
findings.evidence: mild splenomegaly measuring 13.33 cm with a focal infarct

panels.rationale: Single coronal contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen/pelvis in a patient with acute myeloid leukemia. The caption reports splenomegaly with a focal splenic infarct and attributes the infarct to leukemic infiltration and impaired splenic perfusion from circulating leukemic blasts. Splenomegaly maps to the AML hepatosplenomegaly vocabulary finding; splenic infarction is included as a proposed finding. This is a real patient radiology image, not a diagram, chart, or control.
panels.attribution_text: Javier-Rojas et al. Simultaneous Onset of Acute Myeloid Leukemia and Decompensated Cirrhosis: A Rare Case.. Cureus 2025. doi:10.7759/cureus.86990. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: Contrast-enhanced computed tomography scan of the abdomen and pelvis Imaging revealed a small, nodular liver contour consistent with cirrhosis, mild splenomegaly measuring 13.33 cm with a focal infarct (red arrow), and minimal ascites. Although not visualized in this image, the portal, hepatic, and splenic veins were noted to be patent. The portal vein measured 13.8 mm in diameter. Features of portal hypertension were present, including large esophageal varices measuring 4.8 mm (not visualized in this image). Given the clinical context of acute myeloid leukemia, the splenic infarction is more likely attributable to leukemic infiltration and impaired splenic perfusion secondary to circulating leukemic blasts, rather than portal hypertension.

plate_findings.evidence: Orbital Myeloid Sarcoma: An Initial Presentation of Acute Myeloid Leukemia With Maturation; immunohistochemical stains demonstrating positivity for CD34 in the tumor cells

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (A, B, C). A: Panel A is an immunohistochemical stain from a patient with orbital myeloid sarcoma showing CD34 positivity, supporting acute myeloid leukemia/myeloid sarcoma. B: Panel B is an immunohistochemical stain from a patient with orbital myeloid sarcoma showing CD117 positivity, supporting acute myeloid leukemia/myeloid sarcoma. C: Panel C is an immunohistochemical stain from a patient with orbital myeloid sarcoma showing myeloperoxidase positivity, supporting acute myeloid leukemia/myeloid sarcoma.
panels.attribution_text: Batista et al. Orbital Myeloid Sarcoma: An Initial Presentation of Acute Myeloid Leukemia With Maturation.. Cureus 2025. doi:10.7759/cureus.77580. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 4.
panels.figure_caption: Immunohistochemical stains demonstrating positivity for (A) CD34, (B) CD117, and (C) MPO. MPO: myeloperoxidase.
in_text_mentions: Histological sections revealed a densely cellular tumor composed of sheets of atypical cells with a high nucleus-to-cytoplasmic ratio. Nuclei were irregularly round or ovoid with prominent nucleolus, open chromatin, and numerous mitotic figures. The cytoplasm was scant and eosinophilic. The cells were arranged diffusely, occasionally with perivascular distribution (Figure 3). Immunohistochemically, the tumor cells were positive for CD34, CD117, and myeloperoxidase (MPO) and focally positive for CD15 (Figure 4).

in_text_mentions: rovided the definitive answer: MS. Immunohistochemical staining confirmed the diagnosis, with strong positivity for myeloperoxidase (MPO), CD34, CD117, terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase (TdT), B-cell lymphoma 2 (BCL2), and CD43 (Figure 2). The cells were negative for CD99, CD3, CD10, CD20, and CD22, effectively excluding lymphoid and other small round blue cell tumors from the differential diagnosis. Bone marrow aspiration and flow cytometry further established a diagnosis of AML with maturation (FAB-M2) and the t (8;21) translocation, with blast cells making up 30%-40% of the bone marrow.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B, C, D). A: H&E section of a spinal extramedullary myeloid sarcoma in a child with AML; architecture supports chloroma/myeloid sarcoma. [raw subtype: myeloid_sarcoma] B: High-power H&E shows blastic morphology consistent with myeloid sarcoma in the reported AML case. [raw subtype: myeloid_sarcoma] C: CD34 immunohistochemistry of the same spinal myeloid sarcoma confirms scattered CD34-positive tumor cells. [raw subtype: myeloid_sarcoma] D: Myeloperoxidase immunohistochemistry demonstrates diffuse granular cytoplasmic positivity in tumor cells, supporting AML/myeloid sarcoma. [raw subtype: myeloid_sarcoma]

panels.figure_caption: Histopathological examination of the surgical specimen A: Medium power view showing a tumoral proliferation forming cohesive sheets and nests set within a fibro-inflammatory stroma (orange arrow) with numerous dilated vascular channels (white arrow) (Hematoxylin-Eosin-Saffron (HES) stain, magnification x 10). B: High power view demonstrating immature blastic cells provided with round or ovoid nuclei, fine chromatin with prominent nucleoli and a slightly basophilic cytoplasm with indistinct boundaries (green arrow) . Mitotic figure and numerous tangible body macrophages (red arrow) with apoptotic bodies are seen (HES stain, magnification x40). C: CD34 stained scattered tumor cells (red arrow). D: Tumor cells showing diffuse granular cytoplasmic staining of myeloperoxydase (blue arrow).
in_text_mentions: Histopathological examination of the surgical specimen confirmed MS as an extramedullary manifestation of AML (Figure 3).

panels.rationale: Single-panel figure of a Leishman-stained peripheral blood smear from a patient with β-thalassemia major complicated by AML; the caption and in-text description explicitly identify a high percentage of blasts with dispersed chromatin, prominent nucleoli and a low nucleus-to-cytoplasm ratio, indicating acute myeloid leukemia. This is a real patient specimen showing a disease-defining hematologic manifestation (myeloblasts), so it is included and attributed to acute_myeloid_leukemia. The blast finding maps to the closest vocabulary key for myeloblasts (myeloblasts in bone marrow); the peripheral-blood location is noted in proposed_findings. No age, ethnicity, skin, or third-party copyright information is provided.

panels.figure_caption: Leishman-stained peripheral blood smear at 40× magnification, showing a high percentage of blasts with prominent nucleoli and low nucleus-to-cytoplasm ratio, indicative of acute myeloid leukemia
in_text_mentions: Laboratory findings are presented in Table 1. Red cell morphology indicated hypochromia, microcytosis, and occasional fragmentation. Morphologically, the blasts were medium to large in size with a low nucleus-to-cytoplasm ratio, dispersed nuclear chromatin, and prominent nucleoli, indicating acute myeloid leukemia (AML), as shown in Figure 1.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B, C, D). A: Panel A (CD3 immunostain) is a real patient tissue section of the colonic myeloid sarcoma; the neoplastic infiltrate is negative for the T-cell marker CD3, which is part of the immunophenotypic confirmation of myeloid lineage in myeloid sarcoma/AML (chloroma). It is included as part of the diagnostic immunophenotyping of the myeloid sarcoma, though by itself it only shows absence of a lymphoid marker, hence the moderate confidence. [raw subtype: myeloid sarcoma (granulocytic sarcoma) of the colon] B: Panel B (CD20 immunostain) is a real patient tissue section from the colonic myeloid sarcoma; negativity for the B-cell marker CD20 excludes a lymphoid neoplasm and supports the myeloid sarcoma (chloroma) diagnosis in this AML patient. [raw subtype: myeloid sarcoma (granulocytic sarcoma) of the colon] C: Panel C shows diffuse CD117 positivity in the extramedullary blastic infiltrate of the ascending colon, the key immunophenotypic marker...

panels.rationale: Single sagittal T2-weighted spinal MRI of a human patient shows a posterior epidural mass causing severe cord compression and edema, consistent with spinal myeloid sarcoma/chloroma in acute myeloid leukemia. The caption and article title specifically support myeloid sarcoma; the arrow annotation is visible. [raw subtype: myeloid sarcoma (granulocytic sarcoma)]
panels.attribution_text: Azizi et al. Spinal Myeloid Sarcoma Revealing Acute Myeloid Leukemia in a Child: A Case Report.. Cureus 2026. doi:10.7759/cureus.113080. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: Preoperative sagittal T2-weighted spinal MRI showing a well-defined posterior epidural mass measuring 12 × 9 × 45 mm and extending from D4 to D6 (white arrow). The lesion appears hyperintense on T2-weighted images and is causing severe spinal cord compression with associated intramedullary T2 hyperintensity, consistent with secondary spinal cord edema due to mass effect. It also extends into the bilateral D4–D5 and D5–D6 neural foramina and is in close contact with the posterior vertebral arches, without evidence of vertebral body involvement.
in_text_mentions: Urgent spinal MRI demonstrated a posterior epidural mass extending from D4 to D6, isointense on T1-weighted images and hyperintense on T2-weighted images, causing severe spinal cord compression with associated spinal cord edema (Figure 1).

in_text_mentions: An eight-year-old boy with no significant past medical history was brought to the outpatient clinic with a one-month history of bilateral proptosis, predominantly affecting the right eye (Figure 1), as the only finding on the physical exam. An MRI confirmed the presence of an expansive iso-enhancing retroocular lesion that compressed the eye (Figure 2). A complete blood count showed thrombocytopenia and leukopenia, which, alongside the MRI findings, warranted a biopsy of the lesion.

panels.rationale: Single axial CT panel from a pediatric case report of orbital myeloid sarcoma (chloroma/granulocytic sarcoma) as the initial presentation of acute myeloid leukemia with maturation. [raw subtype: acute_myeloid_leukemia_with_maturation]

panels.figure_caption: Axial CT Scan of the Orbits Showing Extensive Bilateral Retro-Orbital Masses; The Left Orbit Exhibits Severe Proptosis, and Orbital Wall Erosion Extends Inferiorly and Temporally, Demonstrating the Involvement of the Lacrimal Gland and Extraocular Muscles.
in_text_mentions: Advanced imaging in Jordan revealed extensive bilateral retro-orbital masses involving intra- and extraconal spaces. The tumor had caused severe proptosis and even orbital wall erosion. The masses extended inferiorly and temporally, inseparable from the lacrimal glands and extraocular muscles (Figure 1). Post-contrast CT imaging showed homogeneous enhancement. Imaging the brain, chest, and abdomen revealed no evidence of disease elsewhere.

in_text_mentions: In February 2021, the patient experienced a headache, dizziness, nausea, and gait disturbance and presented to the emergency department of our hospital. Computed tomography (CT) of the head revealed a hyperdense mass in the right cerebellum, significantly compressing the brainstem and fourth ventricle (Figure 1A). Head MRI revealed an extra-axial mass lesion with well-defined borders that did not exhibit contrast enhancement in the right cerebellum (43×43 mm); it was in contact with the dura mater (Figure 1B, 1C). Diffusion-weighted imaging demonstrated no high-intensity signals (Figure 1D).

panels.rationale: Clinical photograph of a real patient's feet showing multiple well-circumscribed hemorrhagic bullae on erythematous bases on both soles, matching the caption. The article title explicitly links these hemorrhagic bullae (with Sweet syndrome) to acute myeloid leukemia with myelodysplasia-related changes, so the panel is attributed to AML as an AML-associated cutaneous manifestation. Hemorrhagic bullae are not directly in the vocabulary; the closest allowed hemorrhagic skin finding is mapped and the specific morphology is proposed. Skin tone judged from the visible feet; no ethnicity or age stated in the caption.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 6 panels (A, B, C, D, E, F). A: Gross image of a small bowel mucosal mass; article and in-text mentions confirm AML infiltration, consistent with extramedullary myeloid tumor/chloroma. B: Gross cut-surface image of the small bowel mass; in-text confirms AML infiltration, consistent with extramedullary myeloid tumor/chloroma. C: Low-power H&E of the small bowel mass; histology and in-text mention support AML infiltration, consistent with extramedullary myeloid tumor/chloroma. D: High-power H&E shows AML blast morphology in small bowel tissue; caption and in-text confirm AML diagnosis. E: H&E shows eroded small bowel mucosa overlying leukemic infiltrate; in-text confirms AML. F: H&E demonstrates AML cells infiltrating through muscularis propria and serosa; in-text confirms AML diagnosis.
panels.attribution_text: Gu et al. Infantile Acute Myeloid Leukemia Presenting As Intussusception: A Case Report and Review of the Literature.. Cureus 2025. doi:10.7759/cureus.96237. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 3.
panels.figure_caption: Macroscopic and microscopic images Gross examination revealed a fungating, tan-red, firm mass on the mucosal surface (A), which is solid on the cut surface (B&C). Microscopically, a hypercellular lesion is underneath the mucosa, composed of a population of moderately sized, irregularly shaped cells with a high N: C ratio. They have coarse chromatin, prominent nucleoli and some visible nuclear grooves (D). The surface mucosa is eroded (E). Tumor cells are infiltrating through the muscularis propria and serosa (F).
in_text_mentions: Histopathology of the small bowel resection showed the bowel mucosa was replaced by a population of moderately sized, irregularly shaped cells with coarse chromatin, prominent nucleoli, and some with visible nuclear grooves, which were consistent with the diagnosis of AML (Figure 3).

panels.rationale: H&E histopathology panel from a case report of intracranial extramedullary relapse of AML presenting as myeloid sarcoma; the caption describes diffuse sheets of uniform small round cells with large nuclei, prominent nucleoli and mitotic figures, and the in-text immunoprofile (CD117+, CD34+, MPO±, Ki-67 ~80%) confirms myeloid lineage, supporting the AML chloroma/myeloid sarcoma finding. No patient age or ethnicity is stated in the caption or in-text. [raw subtype: myeloid sarcoma (granulocytic sarcoma) - intracranial extramedullary relapse]
panels.attribution_text: Cao and Cao. Intracranial extramedullary relapse of acute myeloid leukemia presenting as myeloid sarcoma mimicking meningioma: a case report and literature review.. Frontiers in oncology 2026. doi:10.3389/fonc.2026.1769002. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 4.
panels.figure_caption: Histopathological features. The tumor is composed of diffuse sheets of relatively uniform, small round cells with large, round nuclei, prominent nucleoli, and readily identifiable mitotic figures (original magnification ×10).
in_text_mentions: d grayish-white. Gross total resection was achieved, and no invasion of the underlying cerebral gyri and sulci was observed (Figure 3). Histopathological examination revealed a proliferation of small, round tumor cells (Figure 4). Immunohistochemically, the tumor cells were CD117 (+), CD34 (+), CD68 (+), and MPO (±), a profile consistent with myeloid lineage differentiation. CD56 was only focally positive, and the Ki-67 proliferation index was approximately 80%. The patient recovered well postoperatively, and she was subsequently transferred to the hematology service for systemic chemotherapy.

panels.rationale: Single real-patient axial CT image from a case report of pediatric acute myeloid leukemia presenting with unilateral exophthalmos. The caption describes lacrimal gland infiltration with extraconal extension, an extramedullary orbital manifestation (chloroma/myeloid sarcoma) directly attributable to AML. The image contains a pink annotation arrow.
panels.attribution_text: Erraoui et al. Unilateral Exophthalmos as the Initial Presentation of Acute Myeloid Leukemia in a Pediatric Patient: A Report of a Rare Case.. Cureus 2025. doi:10.7759/cureus.85975. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 2.

plate_findings.evidence: Cervical lymph node biopsy histologic findings consistent with extramedullary AML; "Histology revealed a population of myeloblasts, consistent with extramedullary infiltration of AML (Figure 3)"

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 5 panels (A, B, C, D, E). A: H&E stained cervical lymph node core biopsy showing effacement of nodal architecture by extramedullary AML infiltration; real patient histology consistent with the configured disease. B: Higher-power H&E of the lymph node biopsy showing foci of mononuclear cells with open chromatin (myeloblasts) indicating extramedullary AML; arrows annotate the foci. C: CD34 immunostain of the lymph node core biopsy highlighting blasts, supporting extramedullary AML. D: CD117 immunostain highlighting myeloblasts in the lymph node, confirming myeloid lineage of the extramedullary infiltrate. E: CD10 immunostain demonstrating excess myeloid mononuclear cells consistent with myeloblasts in the lymph node, supporting extramedullary AML.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 9 panels (A, B, C, D, E, F, G, H, I). A: Non-contrast axial CT of the patient's left frontal intracranial myeloid sarcoma (extramedullary AML relapse), showing a hyperdense mass with surrounding edema and mass effect; disease attribution supported by the disease-focused article title and the captioned mass. B: Bone-window CT of the same patient's intracranial myeloid sarcoma; the panel documents absence of hyperostosis/destruction, a negative but tumor-relevant finding in the disease region. C: CT angiography of the patient's intracranial myeloid sarcoma showing mass effect with midline arterial displacement and no tumoral vascular supply; same patient and lesion as the rest of the figure. D: Axial T1-weighted MRI of the patient's intracranial leukemic (myeloid sarcoma) mass; disease attribution from the disease-focused article title plus the captioned, in-text-described CNS lesion in a patient with AML extramedullary relapse. panels.figure_caption: Neuroimaging findings. (A) Non-contrast CT (brain window). (B) Non-contrast CT, bone window, showing no hyperostosis or destruction. (C) CT angiography (CTA) demonstrating displacement of the anterior cerebral artery to the contralateral side, with no evident tumor supply from the internal carotid artery system. (D, E) Axial T1-weighted and T2-weighted MRI showing a well-defined mass that is isointense on T1 and slightly hyperintense on T2, with significant peritumoral edema. (F) Diffusion-weighted image (DWI) showing hyperintensity, indicating restricted diffusion. (G–I) Contrast-enhanced T1-weighted MRI showing strong tumor enhancement and a “dural tail sign”.
in_text_mentions: Cranial magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed an oval-shaped mass in the left frontal region, measuring approximately 5.4×4.9×5.1 cm. The lesion appeared isointense on T1-weighted images (T1WI) and slightly hyperintense on T2-weighted images (T2WI), accompanied by significant peritumoral edema. Contrast-enhanced scans showed marked tumor enhancement with a “dural tail sign”. Notably, diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) demonstrated restricted diffusion (Figure 1).
